q: Where does my oxygen come from?

a.text: From MOXIE: a metal tree that breathes in Martian air.
It makes oxygen out of carbon dioxide at 800 °C.

q: Why is it dangerous outside at night?

a.text: Mars lost its thermal blanket: its atmosphere is razor thin.
At night the temperature plunges to around −80 °C.

q: Which rock should I look for?

a.text: One with layers and spots, just like Cheyava Falls.

q: Why do Earth messages take so long?

a.text: Radio travels at the speed of light, but Mars is millions of kilometers away.
That's why each transmission takes between 3 and 22 minutes to arrive.

q: Why do I have to clean the solar panels?

a.text: Fine Martian dust blocks sunlight and cuts the base's power.
In 2022, dust coated the InSight lander's panels and ended the mission.

q: Why do we wear gloves when handling soil?

a.text: Martian regolith contains perchlorates, toxic salts.
With our sealed suit and sieve, we can study it safely.
The Sun hurls a fast-moving cloud of energetic particles called a CME.
The shelter's thick regolith walls are your castle shield.
95% is carbon dioxide, and pressure is barely 6 millibars.
That is less than 1% of Earth's atmospheric pressure.

q: Where is water hiding in Jezero?

a.text: Jezero has no exposed ice sitting on the surface.
Water stayed locked inside clays and hydrated minerals.

q: Do all solar storms hit Mars?

a.text: Not all of them: space is huge, and many CMEs miss the planet.
NASA's WSA-Enlil model helps forecast which path they'll take.
